quotes.full: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius
quotes.context: Private notes a Roman emperor wrote to himself while on campaign.
quotes.moral: Treat the obstacle as the path — resistance can become fuel.

quotes.full: Confine yourself to the present.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius
quotes.context: Stoic counsel against living in past regret or future anxiety.
quotes.moral: Work with what is here now; the rest is not yours to hold.

quotes.short: You have power over your mind
quotes.full: You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
quotes.author: Marcus Aurelius
quotes.context: Core Stoic split between what you control and what you don’t.
quotes.moral: Strength is mastery of judgment, not mastery of the world.

quotes.full: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
quotes.author: Seneca
quotes.context: Advice from a Roman statesman to a friend on needless fear.
quotes.moral: Most pain arrives early as rehearsal — don’t live the disaster twice.

quotes.full: Begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
quotes.author: Seneca
quotes.context: On treating time as the one resource you cannot store.
quotes.moral: Start now; make today complete on its own terms.

quotes.short: we waste a lot of it
quotes.full: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.
quotes.author: Seneca
quotes.context: Essay arguing busyness and distraction shrink a life more than years do.
quotes.moral: Life feels short when attention is spent poorly.

quotes.short: Make the best use of what
quotes.full: Make the best use of what is in your power, and take the rest as it happens.
quotes.author: Epictetus
quotes.context: Handbook of a former slave turned Stoic teacher.
quotes.moral: Act where you have leverage; accept what you don’t.

quotes.full: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.
quotes.author: Epictetus
quotes.context: Foundational Stoic claim about judgment as the source of upset.
quotes.moral: Change the story you tell about the event, and the event softens.

quotes.full: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.
quotes.author: Richard Feynman
quotes.context: Caltech commencement talk on scientific integrity and self-deception.
quotes.moral: Doubt your own cleverness first; honesty starts there.

quotes.full: What I cannot create, I do not understand.
quotes.author: Richard Feynman
quotes.context: Left on his office blackboard near the end of his life.
quotes.moral: True understanding is the ability to rebuild from scratch.

quotes.full: I would rather have questions that can't be answered than answers that can't be questioned.
quotes.author: Richard Feynman
quotes.context: Widely attributed line capturing his stance on open inquiry.
quotes.moral: Prefer live questions over sealed answers.

quotes.short: Good prose is like a windowpane
quotes.full: Good prose is like a windowpane.
quotes.author: George Orwell
quotes.context: On prose that disappears so the subject can be seen clearly.
quotes.moral: Write to reveal, not to decorate.

quotes.full: To see what is in front of one's nose needs a constant struggle.
quotes.author: George Orwell
quotes.context: Essay on how ideology and habit hide the obvious.
quotes.moral: Obvious facts still require deliberate attention.

quotes.full: The great enemy of clear language is insincerity.
quotes.author: George Orwell
quotes.context: His essay linking muddy prose to dishonest thought.
quotes.moral: Vague words usually protect a vague intention.

quotes.full: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
quotes.author: Joan Didion
quotes.context: Opening of an essay on narrative as a way to hold chaos together.
quotes.moral: Meaning is made — notice the story you’re living by.

quotes.short: to find out what I'm thinking
quotes.full: I write entirely to find out what I'm thinking, what I'm looking at, what I see and what it means.
quotes.author: Joan Didion
quotes.context: Didion on writing as discovery rather than transcription.
quotes.moral: Put words down to learn what you mean.

quotes.full: Live the questions now.
quotes.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
quotes.context: Counsel to a young writer impatient for certainty.
quotes.moral: Don’t force answers; inhabit the questions until they ripen.

quotes.full: Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves as if they were locked rooms or books written in a very foreign language.
quotes.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
quotes.context: Same letter cycle — patience with unresolved inner life.
quotes.moral: Treat unanswered things as rooms to enter, not problems to crush.

quotes.full: The man who moves a mountain begins by carrying away small stones.
quotes.author: Confucius
quotes.context: Popular saying in the Confucian tradition on gradual effort.
quotes.moral: Huge work is just many small, unbroken moves.

quotes.full: Real knowledge is to know the extent of one's ignorance.
quotes.author: Confucius
quotes.context: Often linked to Analects themes on humility in learning.
quotes.moral: Knowing what you don’t know is the start of wisdom.

quotes.full: How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.
quotes.author: Annie Dillard
quotes.context: From her book on the daily discipline of making work.
quotes.moral: Your life is the sum of ordinary days — spend them on purpose.

quotes.full: One of the few things I know about writing is this: spend it all, shoot it, play it, lose it, all, right away, every time.
quotes.author: Annie Dillard
quotes.context: On not hoarding your best material for later.
quotes.moral: Use the good idea now; more will come.

quotes.full: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
quotes.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
quotes.context: Closing proposition of his early work on the limits of saying.
quotes.moral: Don’t force language past what it can honestly hold.

quotes.full: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
quotes.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
quotes.context: Early Wittgenstein on language as the boundary of thinkable world.
quotes.moral: Widen your words and you widen what you can see.
